summary: The paper pre-registers and tests whether Guo et al. (2017)'s finding that calibration worsens with capacity in large networks also holds at the opposite end of the capacity spectrum (2-128 hidden unit MLPs). Across three binary classification datasets (two-moons, circles, Wisconsin breast cancer), 7 widths, and 10 seeds each (210 trained models), the pre-registered hypothesis is rejected in the opposite direction: ECE before temperature scaling decreases significantly with width in all three datasets, and the effect survives a partial-correlation control for the confounding accuracy-width relationship. The authors also report a training-set ECE diagnostic consistent with an underfitting-relief mechanism, a convergence-confound check, leave-one-width-out robustness, and honest underpowered-null reporting for the temperature-scaling result on two of three datasets.
strengths:
- I reran experiment.py from scratch (bit-identical fixed-seed re-execution) and every reported number reproduces exactly: H1 Spearman ρ = -0.523/-0.762/-0.357 with p = 0.0000/0.0000/0.0030, H2 Wilcoxon p and rank-biserial values, and H3 all matched analysis.json and the paper's tables to full float precision. I also verified followup_analysis.json's partial correlations (-0.471/-0.737/-0.316) and convergence counts (2 of 210, both circles widths 4 and 8) match the paper's claims exactly, and robustness.json's leave-one-out range for circles (-0.70 to -0.79) matches the text.
- The accuracy-confound check (partial rank correlation controlling for test accuracy) directly addresses the most obvious alternative explanation for the width-ECE trend, and it is done correctly (rank-residual partial Spearman), not just asserted.
- Reporting is unusually honest about its own limits: it explicitly flags the two null H2 results as underpowered (effect size below the study's own pre-computed MDE) rather than claiming temperature scaling 'doesn't work', and the discussion repeatedly narrows the title's claim to the specific studied corner of the design space rather than overclaiming a general theory of small-network calibration.
weaknesses:
- The empirical contribution is narrow by the authors' own admission: one architecture family (single-hidden-layer sklearn MLPClassifier/Adam), three low-dimensional-or-small-n datasets, and only one post-hoc calibration method. This limits how much the 'non-monotonic width-calibration relationship across the full capacity axis' framing in the discussion can be supported — the paper has no data between width 128 and the large-model regime, so the 'unlocated turning point' claim, while appropriately hedged, is speculative narrative rather than evidence.
- The partial correlation used to rule out the accuracy confound is a rank-based linear control, not a causal design (e.g., matching runs on accuracy across widths and comparing ECE directly); the paper acknowledges this but the underfitting-relief 'mechanism' claim still rests more on correlational plausibility (training ECE and test ECE both fall with width) than on an intervention that isolates capacity from data-fit.
- Related-work coverage is thin (5 references) for a paper whose central move is contrasting with an established literature; specific comparable studies on calibration under underfitting/regularization or double-descent-style non-monotonicity in calibration (e.g., Mukhoti et al. 2020 on focal loss and calibration, or more recent small-model/tabular calibration studies) are not engaged individually, only gestured at qualitatively in one sentence.
questions:
1. Since the synthetic datasets (moons/circles) are redrawn with a different random draw for every (width, seed) combination rather than holding one fixed dataset per replicate across all widths, could you comment on whether this adds meaningful variance to the width-ECE estimate, and did you check whether results change if the same 10 data draws are reused across all 7 widths?
2. Do you have any indication of where the 'turning point' between the underfitting-relief regime and the Guo et al. overconfidence regime might lie, even roughly (e.g. does extending to width 256 or 512 already show ECE flattening or reversing)?
3. Why was Bonferroni correction applied with denominator 6 rather than treating H1 and H3 as separate families or applying a per-family correction — was this decided in the pre-registration, and would the breast-cancer H1 result (p=0.003) survive a stricter correction if H2's tests were also included in the same family?
